uncited: This method derives analytical Jacobians of the SE(3) camera pose with respect to 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) primitives to enable efficient gradient-based camera tracking.
It solves the problem of high computational overhead and redundant parameterization inherent in automatic differentiation when optimizing camera poses in SLAM systems.

Unlike prior ray-intersection methods that assume fewer Gaussians, this approach provides the first analytical Jacobians for EWA splatting and 3DGS, ensuring the Jacobian dimensionality matches the six degrees of freedom of the Lie algebra.
*   **Input:** Camera pose $T_{CW} \in SE(3)$, 3D Gaussian parameters (mean $\mu_W$, covariance $\Sigma_W$, opacity $\alpha$, color $\mathbf{c}$).
*   **Output:** Jacobians $\frac{\partial \mu_I}{\partial T_{CW}}$ and $\frac{\partial \Sigma_I}{\partial T_{CW}}$ required for gradient descent optimization of the camera pose.
where $\mathbf{T} \in SE(3)$, $\tau \in se(3)$, and $\circ$ is group composition.
where $J$ is the Jacobian of the perspective projection.
The Gaussian mean in camera coordinates is $\mu_C = R_{CW} \mu_W + t_{CW}$.
Let $\mathbf{T} = T_{CW}$ and perturb it by $\text{Exp}(\tau)$ where $\tau = [\theta, \rho]^T$.
Let $W$ be the rotation component of $T_{CW}$.
Perturb the rotation part of the Lie algebra by $\theta$.
The derivative of the rotation matrix $W$ with respect to the rotation vector components is derived from $\frac{\partial W}{\partial \theta_i} = e_i^\times W$, where $e_i$ are basis vectors.
Substitute the manifold derivatives into the chain rule equations.
The term $\frac{\partial \mu_I}{\partial \mu_C}$ and $\frac{\partial J}{\partial \mu_C}$ are standard differentiable projection operations.
The term $\frac{\partial \Sigma_I}{\partial W}$ accounts for the rotation of the 3D covariance into the camera frame.
This variant optimizes only the current camera pose without updating the map representation.

It minimizes photometric residuals $E_{pho} = \| I(\mathcal{G}, \mathbf{T}_{CW}) - \bar{I} \|_1$ and/or geometric residuals $E_{geo} = \| D(\mathcal{G}, \mathbf{T}_{CW}) - \bar{D} \|_1$, where $I$ is the rendered image and $D$ is the depth rasterization.
It optimizes affine brightness parameters for exposure variation and penalizes non-edge or low-opacity pixels.

The depth rasterization is computed via alpha-blending: $\mathcal{D}_p = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}} z_i \alpha_i \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha_j)$, where $z_i$ is the distance to the Gaussian mean along the camera ray.
*   **Time Complexity:** The analytical derivation eliminates the overhead of automatic differentiation, making view synthesis and gradient computation computationally efficient.
Unifies tracking, mapping, and novel view synthesis.
*   **Limitations:** Requires careful keyframe management to avoid infeasible joint optimization of all poses and Gaussians.
This method originates from the Gaussian Splatting SLAM paper, which introduced the first analytical Jacobians of SE(3) camera pose with respect to 3D Gaussians used in EWA splatting and 3DGS.
Prior methods assumed fewer Gaussians and relied on ray-intersection, making them inapplicable to 3DGS.
